question: During phacoemulsification surgery, a piece of the nuclus was difficult to be taken to the AC and other small pieces floating rapidly in AC. What to do?
explanation: Categorize: adjusting the aspiration flow rate can help attract nuclear or cortical material into the aspiration port of the phaco tip or irrigation/aspiration handpiece. Compared with low-compliance tubing, high-compliance tubing collapses more easily as vacuum builds, leading to a greater surge once occlusion has been broken and the tubing rebounds to an uncollapsed state. Followability A qualitative descriptor for how quickly and easily fragments are attracted to and held at the aspiration port. Distal followability (how quickly fragments are attracted to the aspiration port) is improved by increasing the aspiration flow rate. Proximal followability (how easily fragments are held at the aspiration port) is improved by increasing both aspiration flow rate (in the case of partial occlusion) and vacuum (in cases of partial and complete occlusion). Infusion pressure The pressure of the fluid coming through the irrigation tubing. It is controlled either by the irrigation bottle height (on a gravity-based machine) or by the intraocular pressure (IOP) setting (on a saline bag compression-based machine). Irrigation The influx of fluid into the eye, which is related to the infusion pressure. Occlusion An obstruction of the aspiration port or aspiration tubing that causes vacuum to build until it reaches the machine's preset value or until the material is evacuated. Rise time The time it takes for vacuum to build to a given level once the aspiration port has been occluded. Surge (or postocclusion surge) An undesirable phenomenon that occurs when vacuum has built up because of an occlusion and the occlusion is suddenly broken, causing the fluid in the higher-pressure (positive) anterior chamber to rush into the lower-pressure (negative) aspiration tubing. When the sudden egress of fluid exceeds the influx capability of the irrigation line, sudden shallowing of the anterior chamber may occur, and the iris or posterior capsule may be drawn into the aspiration port. Surge can be minimized by increased infusion pressure (ie, increased irrigation), lower vacuum, low-compliance tubing of smaller diameter, a smaller aspiration port, coiled aspiration tubing, and occlusion-mode software (including automatic modification of irrigation and aspiration flow rate). Vacuum The magnitude of negative pressure created in the aspiration tubing, measured in millimeters of mercury (mm Hg). Vacuum builds when the aspiration port is occluded, providing a gripping force; its strength determines how strongly particulate material will be held. Vacuum limit The maximum level of vacuum that a pump can produce upon complete occlusion of the aspiration port. (Scenario of chatter during Phaco. You need to increase the vacuum, decrease the power or using different power modulation like pulse mode) Chatter This undesirable phenomenon occurs when the repulsive force of the ultrasonic stroke overcomes the vacuum, or "holding power" This process causes the nuclear fragments to be repelled by the ultrasonic tip until the vacuum reaches a level sufficient to neutralize this repulsive energy and once again hold the material. This back-and-forth movement of lens material from the tip impairs followability (see the Glossary of Fluid-is and Phacodynamics Terminology). Chatter can be diminished by reducing the phaco power (ie, by decreasing the stroke length of the tip), thereby reducing the forces that push a fragment away from the tip. question: A 87 year old present to you with a deep A/C, high IOP and hypermature cataract, no KPs, what is the dx?
explanation: Categorized: Glaucoma Phacolytic glaucoma is one of the 4 lens-induced glaucomas. The other three are phacomorphic glaucoma, lens particle glaucoma, and phacoantigenic glaucoma. Phacolytic glaucoma occurs in the presence of a mature or hypermature cataract. In these cataracts, there is an increased concentration of high molecular weight lens protein. These proteins are released through microscopic openings in the lens capsule (i.e. not trauma/surgery induced) and clog up the trabecular meshwork. In addition, macrophages (i.e. the "refractile bodies") phagocytize these large proteins and also clog up the trabecular meshwork. This combination of factors leads to an acute rise in intraocular pressure. The BCSC states that some of distinguishing features of phacolytic glaucoma are: lack of keratic precipitates(which are found in phacoantigenic glaucoma), an open angle (contrast this with the closed angle in phacomorphic glaucoma), and a macroscopically-intact lens capsule (contrast this with lens-particle glaucoma which often involves a violated lens capsule). Phacoanaphylactic uveitis (also known as phacoantigenic uveitis) occurs when the capsular bag is violated which leads to inflammation. Phacomorphic glaucoma occurs when the lens becomes so large that it pushes the iris forward and closes the angle. The treatment is surgical removal of the lens. Both phacolytic and phacoantigenic glaucomas can present with a hot eye that contains a hypermature cataract. However, lack of keratic precipitates is more characteristic of phacolytic glaucoma. Cytology of aqueous would reveal lens-laden macrophages in phacolytic glaucoma. Phacomorphic glaucoma would present with a shallow anterior chamber while lens particle glaucoma would present with MACROscopic lens pieces in the anterior chamber (in contrast to MICROscopic lens proteins as in phacolytic glaucoma). question: What is the spherical equivalent of +1.00 - 2.00 x 90?
explanation: The spherical equivalent is the dioptric power of the circle of least confusion for a spherocylindrical lens. In other words, the spherical equivalent is the dioptric midpoint of a spherocylindrical lens where the horizontal and vertical dimensions of the blurred image are approximately equal. The goal of refraction is to choose a lens that places the circle of least confusion on the retina. Spherical equivalent is calculated by adding the sphere and half of the cylinder. question: What type of astigmatism does a patient with a refraction of + 1.00 + 2.00 x 75 degrees have?
explanation: Astigmatism is typically caused by a toric-shaped cornea. Regular astigmatism is present when one meridian of the cornea is the flattest and perpendicular (90 degrees away) from one meridian that is the steepest. With-the-rule astigmatism, the more common type of astigmatism in children, is corrected with a plus cylinder between 60 and 120 degrees. In against-the-rule astigmatism, the astigmatism can be corrected with a plus cylinder between 150 and 30 degrees. Oblique astigmatism is corrected with a plus cylinder between 31 to 59 and 121 to 149 degrees. In irregular astigmatism, the steep and flat meridians of the cornea are not perpendicular to each other. In these patients, cylindrical lenses often do little to improve vision, and rigid gas permeable contact lenses should be tried to reach best vision. One way of classifying astigmatism is by the location of the focal lines within the eye. Simple astigmatism refers to one focal line on the retina and one line either in front of the retina (simple myopic astigmatism) or behind the retina (simple hyperopic astigmatism). In compound astigmatism, both focal lines are either in front of the retina (compound myopic astigmatism) or behind the retina (compound hyperopic astigmatism). In mixed astigmatism, the focal lines are on both sides of the retina (straddling the retina). Transcribed from a screenshot in the source document.
